Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says
Ukrainian president says Kyiv not ready to concede Donbas but would put idea to a referendum in exchange for security guarantees and funding. What we know on day 1,726
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member . But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’,” he said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. “That is why ⁠I believe Nato is back on the agenda.” But he said the suggestion, which would form part of a new postwar security framework for Europe, could allow Russia to weaken Nato and reshape borders. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded ​Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a ‌national referendum. Echoing comments ‌made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are ‌agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. “We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.
The Ukrainian president has also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality , something that could only happen if the country’s constitution was changed. “If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in Nato right now anyway.”
US President ⁠Donald Trump’s ⁠envoy and ​son-in-law Jared ⁠Kushner said on ⁠Saturday ​the US ‌was ‌focused on ‌facilitating direct engagement between Russia and ‌European nations on ​the Ukraine war , ⁠after trilateral meetings ​involving Washington, ​Moscow ​and ​Kyiv ‌this ​week. However, Washington and Nato have not yet commented on the suggestion of a swap of the Donbas for Ukraine Nato membership. Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.
Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system , saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”. Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones, in place for five days, meant they could no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones. Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Putin.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an “unjust peace” and warned that it was a recipe for another war . “Those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it” and, by extension, all of Europe, Macron said on social media. “That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France’s position.”
Russian forces ⁠struck a cargo vessel in ⁠the ⁠Ukrainian ​port of Chornomorsk , RIA ⁠news agency cited the Russian ⁠defence ministry ​as ‌saying on ‌Saturday. The ministry ‌said the ship was being used to supply the Ukrainian ‌military. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on the Samara oil pipeline station near the village of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region on Friday set several oil storage tanks on fire, Ukraine’s General Staff said. The facility is a key part of the network exporting Russian oil to global markets, the General Staff said. Separately, 22 people were injured in a Russian attack on the south-east Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Friday, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.

items.title: U.S. facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia amid push for peace in Ukraine, Kushner says - CBS News
items.summary: U.S. facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia amid push for peace in Ukraine, Kushner says  CBS News
items.content:
The United States is facilitating direct engagement between Russia and Europe amid a push to secure a peace deal in the war in Ukraine , President Trump's special envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Saturday.
Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this past week as the Trump administration pushes to end the more than 4 ½-year conflict. The meetings came after the first round of U.S.-brokered talks between the two countries since February concluded on Wednesday with an announcement of plans for a new prisoner exchange and further talks, but nothing to suggest a wider peace deal.
"Our focus is now on facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks," Kushner said in a social media post on Saturday. "Several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored. Some may lead to breakthroughs directly, while others may evolve into new proposals that help bridge the remaining gaps."
Zelenskyy, in statements released Saturday, said the U.S. had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe, though he warned that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent's borders.
"In my view, this can be dangerous," Zelenskyy told reporters Friday, referring to the new security framework. "This should not be the main agenda." His comments were embargoed until Saturday.
Zelenskyy said the U.S. had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to NATO. He reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory.
He also said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the war.
"Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."
European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent's security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate NATO's future.
Ukraine is discussing a comprehensive security package with its partners that could include specific guarantees from NATO and the European Union, a strong Ukrainian military and financial support for a specified period, he said. It would also include a recovery plan, he said.
"If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: Do we accept it or not?" Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian.
Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution.
"If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in NATO right now anyway."
Kushner said Saturday that a lasting peace in Ukraine requires security guarantees for Kyiv and "detailed, actionable postwar security arrangements that reduce the risk of another war."
"NATO will remain a critical pillar of European security, enhanced by stronger mechanisms for military, communication, deconfliction, and reciprocal de-escalation, with practical ways to address disputes before they become crises," he added. "This is why we are working to bring our European partners directly into these discussions. Any final agreement must be agreed to by the relevant parties, and President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine's and Europe's security and make future conflict less likely."
Zelenskyy warned that broader discussions about Europe's security could allow Putin to seek changes to NATO's military presence, including the withdrawal of American troops.
He said Putin had raised similar ideas with then-President Joe Biden in 2021, seeking a redistribution of power in Europe and the world.
"I think Putin will bring up Finland and Sweden. I'm sure he will raise the issue of Hungary and the presence of American troops in the Baltic countries," Zelenskyy said.
He said any changes to Europe's security arrangements must be decided by European NATO members only after the war ends.
"The sequence should be as follows: a ceasefire, an end to the war in Ukraine, and security guarantees for Ukraine," he said. "There can be no security guarantees in Europe, or for Europe, without Ukraine."
Mr. Trump is set to meet with Putin next week as part of a trilateral summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. He is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, officials said.

US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to advance peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.

US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not believe it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled openness to negotiations with Europe, but has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom – have signalled a readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said that the Russian “acceptance, as it has been accepted by Jared Kushner of European participation [in the talks], is something that could actually be important”.
“Kushner makes direct reference as well to the issue of security guarantees required by Ukraine, and he makes clear that it would be NATO that would provide these guarantees,” Hanna said.
Moreover, he added, “as negotiators are suggesting, there might be another round of multilateral negotiations to build on what’s been called ‘substantial progress’ in the recent talks”.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said Europe must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Moscow’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

2 oil tankers hit mines, catch fire near Strait of Hormuz: Iran's Revolutionary Guard
2 oil tankers hit mines, catch fire near Strait of Hormuz: Iran's Revolutionary Guard
Iranian naval force says vessels were attempting to pass through waterway undetected along what it called ‘an unauthorized route’
ISTANBUL Two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said early Sunday.
In a statement, the force said the vessels were attempting to pass through the waterway undetected along what it called an unauthorized route, with their navigation and automatic identification systems switched off.
The Iranian naval force said the mine strikes triggered explosions and large fires aboard the tankers.
The statement did not identify the vessels or provide information about possible casualties.
The Revolutionary Guard's naval force had reported Friday that two oil tankers struck mines and caught fire while attempting to use an “unauthorized route” through the southern part of the strait.
It also warned shipping companies against attempting passage without coordinating with its maritime traffic control center.
The incidents come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway for global energy and commodity supplies.
Navigation through the strait has also been a key issue in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before the sides reached a ceasefire in April.
Fighting between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled, despite the two sides signing a memorandum of understanding in June.

items.title: Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share Russian casualties ‘reach 450,000’: What that means for the Ukraine war on social media
A member of the 'Platsdarm' volunteer group recovers the bodies of deceased Ukrainian and Russian military personnel [File: Chris McGrath/Getty]
Records leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, have shown that at least 450,000 Russians, most of them soldiers, died in the war in Ukraine up to August this year.
Among the dead were more than 4,000 foreign citizens who are believed to have died fighting for Russia, from countries including Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Nepal, Colombia and Nigeria.
The records were obtained by two hacking groups, the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Ukraine’s Silent Crow.
Rosstat confirmed it had been hit by cyberattacks between October 29 and November 1, but said it found no evidence that its databases had been compromised or that protected data leaked.
Moscow does not officially publish its military death toll.
Deaths can take months, and sometimes years, to be registered, in Russia. Investigations for The Financial Times (FT) have concluded that once late paperwork is counted, the toll up to August will settle at about 550,000.
So what do the leaked records show, and what do they tell us about who is fighting Russia’s war? Here’s what you need to know:
The Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow said on November 1 that they had broken into Rosstat’s network.
The two hacking groups published their own analysis of the records and shared the files with several news organisations, though the data has not been independently verified.
However, media outlets and analysts say they believe it is real.
Janis Kluge, an expert on Russia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, wrote on X: “There is no longer any doubt that the leaked Rosstat database is authentic. You can find any famous person who has died in recent years.”
However, in a later post he added: “The trickier question is: Was the data manipulated to increase the war death toll?” before adding, “This would [be] unbelievably difficult, so this is a highly unlikely conspiracy theory”.
A death toll far beyond anything Moscow has admitted so far.
The files list about 410,000 deaths directly as war-related, and 42,000 more fighting-age men whose deaths were confirmed in court because their bodies have never been recovered.
The FT identified another 12,000 likely military deaths among men who died at or near the front, bringing the total to at least 450,000.
(Al Jazeera) Where have most of those Russian casualties occurred?
About 120,000 of those with a recorded location died in the area containing Avdiivka and Pokrovsk, and a further 48,000 in Bakhmut, the FT reported.
Avdiivka is a small industrial city in the Donetsk region. After Russian-backed forces seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014 and 2015, it became part of the so-called “contact line”, and Ukrainian forces spent years fortifying the city.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it was the subject of two years of bitter fighting before Russia took it in 2024.
After the fall of Avdiivka, Russian forces moved towards the coal-mining city of Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, capturing it in early 2026 after more than a year of gruelling battles that had left the city in ruins.
Bakhmut, a city in the Donetsk Oblast and situated at a vital intersection connecting eastern Ukraine with the rest of the country, was the site of the longest and bloodiest infantry battle of the war before falling to Russian and paramilitary Wagner Group forces in May 2023.
People attend a fundraising event in Ruaka Town, Kiambu County, Kenya, for Grace Gathoni Kagombe, the widow of Martin Macharia Mburu, who was killed fighting in Ukraine for Russia after accepting a civilian job offer [File: Ed Ram/Getty] Who has been killed?
The average age of those killed rose from 34 in the first year of the war to 40 in 2025, and men aged 35 to 44 made up the largest group, with 158,000 dead, the FT reported.
Ethnic Russians constitute more than two-thirds of Russia’s population of 143 million. The rest are minorities – from millions of ethnic Ukrainians and Tatars to smaller Indigenous groups in Siberia and the Arctic.
Zabaykalsky Krai, home to a large community of Buryats, an Indigenous Mongolic people of southern Siberia, recorded about 12,300 deaths, roughly one for every 80 people in the region, the FT reported.
Bashkortostan, another region with a large minority population including Indigenous Bashkirs and Volga Tatars, recorded 15,800 deaths.
The FT identified 4,141 probable foreign soldiers holding foreign citizenship among the dead.
Bloomberg News, using a wider definition that includes people born outside Russia, counted 11,335, with foreign deaths rising from about 630 in 2022 to more than 5,500 in 2025.
Deaths of Nepalis were concentrated in 2023 and 2024, and those of Colombians, Kenyans and Nigerians from late 2025, Bloomberg reported.
The FT counted the highest death toll from Uzbekistan at 807, followed by Tajikistan with 598. There were also 44 Nepali dead and 98 Colombians, the highest toll from Latin America.
About 340 Africans are among the dead, most of them killed since 2025, Bloomberg reported.
Nigeria, Cameroon and Egypt had the highest tolls, with 127 deaths between them, according to the FT.
Furthermore, Ukrainian officials believe Russia deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to hold off Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region, but they do not appear in the leaked data.
Mostly for the money, and often after being misled.
An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army overall.
An Amnesty International report in September found that people from Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa had been promised well-paid civilian jobs and then forced into the army on arrival in Russia.
The rights group spoke with foreign nationals currently serving with Russian forces and members of their families as well as lawyers, human rights activists and journalists.
It found local agents and misleading online job advertisements were being used to deceive foreign nationals in their home countries.
Nationals from 36 African countries are known to be fighting for Russia in the four-year war, Ukraine’s foreign minister said in November last year.
One South African man who applied online for a driving job in Poland was told to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck, and drive it to Poland.
His wife told Amnesty International: “Upon arrival to Moscow, everything was taken from him. He was told that he would not be going to Poland and that he is becoming a soldier.”
Many recruits were promised lucrative salaries and sign-up bonuses that were not then fulfilled, Amnesty reported.
In Kenya , where intelligence officials say more than 1,000 citizens have been recruited, agencies promised monthly wages of about $2,715 and bonuses of up to $9,309.
What do these casualty figures mean for the war in Ukraine?
They indicate that Russia is struggling for manpower.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, posted an analysis of the leaked data, saying the figures likely understate Russia’s true losses because of reporting limitations.
It added that, as of July, Russia’s casualties are now outpacing its recruitment.
Kluge told The Moscow Times that the deaths also represent about half a per cent of Russia’s working-age population, which may have little economic impact, so the main significance is political.
He added, “You cannot say Russia is winning this war if it is losing population at this rate.”

Brussels Prepares to Confront Beijing Over China’s Support for Russia’s War Economy
1.4K European defence ministers will discuss the security implications of relations with China next week as concerns mount over Beijing’s contribution to Russia’s military-industrial capabilities and Europe’s dependence on Chinese technology and materials.
The meeting, scheduled for 17th November in Brussels, will be chaired by EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas.
According to the official Foreign Affairs Council defence agenda , ministers will examine security challenges and strategic dependencies arising from relations with China before discussing military assistance to Ukraine and transatlantic defence cooperation.
The discussions come as the European Commission prepares its next sanctions package against Russia.
Euronews reported on Friday that Kallas intends to raise concerns about Chinese dual-use technology supplied to Russia and reports of Chinese involvement in training Russian military personnel.
Europe’s relationship with China has traditionally been shaped by economic considerations.
China remains a substantial market for European manufacturers and an important supplier of industrial equipment, electronic components and critical materials.
However, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has challenged the assumption that European commercial relations with Beijing can be managed separately from security policy.
In October, the European Parliament adopted a recommendation on EU–China political relations , calling for a coordinated European response to China’s economic practices and its support for Russia.
The recommendation also expressed concern about reports that Russian soldiers had received military training in China.
As EU Today reported at the time, Parliament’s proposals for a tougher China policy combined demands for stronger economic safeguards with continued diplomatic engagement.
The forthcoming ministerial discussions will test the extent to which national governments support that approach.
European measures against Chinese entities accused of supporting Russia’s military industry have become increasingly extensive.
The EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia , adopted in July, extended export restrictions to 51 entities connected to Russia’s military-industrial sector or sanctions circumvention.
Fourteen were based in mainland China or Hong Kong.
Beijing responded immediately by introducing restrictions against 14 European entities, including companies operating in the defence and technology sectors.
In its official explanation of the measures , China’s Ministry of Commerce described the restrictions as a response to European sanctions against Chinese companies.
The inclusion of Rheinmetall, one of Europe’s largest defence manufacturers, demonstrated that Chinese retaliatory export controls could directly affect companies involved in Europe’s military expansion.
The episode exposed a strategic complication: European efforts to restrict supplies reaching Russia may prompt Beijing to restrict supplies required by European industry.
The scale of Europe’s commercial relationship with China limits the scope for rapid disengagement.
The Council’s latest overview of EU–China trade and investment puts European goods exports to China at approximately €199.5 billion in 2025, against imports exceeding €570 billion.
European companies also maintain substantial investments in Chinese manufacturing operations.
These relationships create vulnerabilities on both sides, but the consequences of disruption would vary considerably between member states.
Countries with extensive automotive, pharmaceutical and engineering interests in China may face different pressures from governments whose economic exposure is smaller.
Defence manufacturing presents an additional difficulty because alternative suppliers for certain specialised materials and components cannot always be established quickly.
The effectiveness of European policy will depend partly on whether sanctions are accompanied by measures addressing the industrial dependencies that make retaliation possible.
Greater diversification, investment in domestic production and closer cooperation with alternative suppliers could reduce those vulnerabilities.
Brussels must also ensure that restrictions distinguish between legitimate civilian commerce and activities that materially contribute to Russia’s military capabilities.
A broad deterioration in commercial relations would impose considerable costs without necessarily producing a corresponding reduction in Russian military production.
Tuesday’s discussions will therefore concern more than the contents of the next sanctions package.
Europe must establish whether it can maintain economic relations with China while limiting Beijing’s contribution to the principal military threat facing European security.
Without reducing its own strategic dependencies, the EU risks finding that its capacity to exercise economic pressure remains constrained by the interests of the industries it is seeking to protect.

items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
items.summary: Trump will discuss the "reduction of nuclear weapons" during the unprecedented talks, a spokeswoman says.
items.content:
Image caption, The leaders of the US, Russia and China will meet late next week, according to the White House
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China , which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China's AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?
FAA telecom problems that triggered the ground stop were so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action
Delta CEO says air traffic control systems are so outdated that some commercial flight routes were faster in the 1950s than they are today

The Fed’s battle against inflation risks turning into a forever war—and may last as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom while Iran ‘status quo’ drags on
Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a press conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, on October 28, 2026 in Washington, DC. Al Drago/Getty Images
In a few months, the Federal Reserve will be able to count six years that inflation has been above its 2% target, and central bankers’ own forecasts put “mission accomplished” sometime in 2029.
That means the Fed could fall short on the price-stability portion of its dual mandate for eight straight years—or as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom lasted.
Despite the obvious differences with the bloody Iraq war, the Fed’s inflation fight is also driven by events in the Middle East, this time in Iran.
Inflation was trending lower at the start of the year, as the initial spike from President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year was wearing off. Then crude prices soared after Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz and attacked regional energy infrastructure in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes.
While oil exports have rebounded with the help of U.S. military protection, supplies of refined products like gasoline and diesel remain tight, inflicting more pain at the pump for consumers.
At the same time, GDP growth is running hot as the AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars a year into the economy, adding more pressure on prices.
This past week’s consumer price index for October came in hotter than expected and showed that inflation is spreading beyond energy categories into more goods and services, alarming Fed officials.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the data “borderline disturbing,” and fellow policymakers have indicated more rate hikes are needed, possibly even a jumbo-sized increase of 50 basis points.
Meanwhile, the Iran war shows no signs of ending soon. Trump has backed down from repeated threats to restart major combat operations, but has also shot down negotiations, saying the U.S. doesn’t need a peace deal with Iran.
“We’re just keeping it the status quo,” Trump told reporters on Monday.
With the Iran conflict dragging on indefinitely, the Fed may have to readjust its inflation outlook again and get more aggressive on rates.
In September, the Fed’s summary of economic projections put down 2029 as the year when inflation is expected to fall back to 2%, pushing it back from a 2028 forecast made in June, as energy prices stayed high.
To be sure, there have been several shocks outside the Fed’s control since inflation first exceeded 2% back in early 2021. The pandemic saw supply-chain snarls and massive fiscal stimulus. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sent oil and gas prices soaring. Then came Trump’s trade war last year and his Iran war this year.
But the Fed has also provided monetary stimulus, and Chairman Kevin Warsh has argued that high inflation is a “choice,” suggesting shocks are no excuse. And the longer inflation stays above target, other central bankers have said they are less willing to be patient about rate hikes and “look through” short-term spikes.
Their fear is that an extended period of high prices will eventually cause consumers to lift their long-term inflation expectations and change currency spending patterns that fuel even more inflation.
That’s why the Fed has sounded more hawkish lately as policymakers look to ensure inflation expectations remain anchored and prevent consumers from believing there’s more tolerance for higher prices.
“I believe that the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility,” Goolsbee told CNBC on Friday. “We’ve been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we’re not making any progress, and if anything, it’s going the wrong way.”
On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller offered a similar message, saying a 50-basis-point rate hike should be considered at the Fed’s December meeting if October core consumer prices rose by 0.3% or more. In fact, they did rise 0.3% from the prior month.
“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he explained.
Also on Tuesday, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in separate remarks that it “may be possible to move more rapidly” than what September’s quarter-point hike and October’s hold have implied. She warned the ​current 3.75%-4.00% policy rate is too low and adds to inflationary pressures.
Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, noted Fed hawks are coalescing as inflation has been too hot for too long—and moving higher.
“Fed is losing its inflation fighting credibility,” she posted on LinkedIn this week. “Consumers who rely mostly on wages, not their stock portfolios, are paying the price.”

Ukraine Says Starshield Restrictions Persist, Hampering Drone Defenses
Ukraine Says Starshield Restrictions Persist, Hampering Drone Defenses
The aftermath of a Russian air strike on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhya on November 14.
WASHINGTON -- Ukraine says restrictions affecting its use of SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system remain widespread, hampering the military’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones near the front line and giving Moscow additional opportunities to strike Ukrainian targets.
Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s top diplomat in Washington, told RFE/RL on November 14 that Ukrainian forces continue to experience disruptions despite repeated tests in multiple directions.
“As of today, I can confirm that the restrictions are effective. These are not isolated cases; they are widespread,” Sienik said.
Trump To Discuss Iran, Nuclear Arms With Putin, Xi At Landmark Summit
“Because of this, we can intercept Russian jet-powered UAVs only after they enter the territory controlled by Ukraine. Hence, we can’t shoot them down immediately near the front line. This gives Russians more leverage which they haven’t had so far.”
“For example, our Bars units operate using Starshield. They shoot down jet-powered Shaheds. Now we can’t shoot them down there, near the front line,” he said. Instead, Ukrainian forces must wait until the drones reach other defensive lines.
Sienik said the disruptions had persisted for five days, with Ukrainian officials conducting daily tests and obtaining the same results.
According to Ukrainian officials who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, SpaceX told the ministry: “We are not imposing any restrictions.”
The company referred to technical issues but did not respond to a follow-up question about the situation in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories, the Ukrainian officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also challenged SpaceX's explanation, saying Kyiv does not believe the disruptions are simply technical problems.
Zelenskyy said Starshield terminals operating in temporarily Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories had been subject to speed restrictions of approximately 161 kilometers per hour for five days.
He said the restrictions had political implications, arguing that limiting the service in occupied territories risked treating those areas differently from the rest of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy: US Floated Trading Donbas For NATO Membership
“If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” Zelenskyy said in remarks released by his office on November 14.
He said he had instructed senior military and foreign ministry officials to pursue the issue with SpaceX and seek the restoration of unrestricted service.
The latest dispute follows a similar episode in October, when Ukrainian officials reported that SpaceX had limited the speed of Starlink and Starshield terminals to approximately 160 kph. Service was reportedly restored on October 24.
SpaceX founder Elon Musk has maintained that Starshield is controlled by the US government, with the military determining restrictions on speed and use and the final authority resting with President Donald Trump. Trump has denied involvement in the restrictions.
The disruptions have also drawn growing concern in Washington, where lawmakers from both parties have questioned the extent of private control over communications systems used in Ukraine's defense.
Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Chris Coons, both members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, have formally asked Musk to preserve all records related to restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink and Starshield.
In a letter made public on November 13, the senators requested documents and communications dating back to September 1, including exchanges involving Musk, SpaceX executives, Ukrainian officials, the White House, and the Pentagon.
They also asked Musk to confirm by November 30 that appropriate safeguards were in place.
Democratic lawmakers in the House also condemned reports of renewed limitations.
Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Adam Smith, the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said any restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield in occupied territories and along the line of contact would be unacceptable if confirmed.
They argued that previous limitations had contributed to Ukrainian civilian casualties, including the deaths of children, and strengthened Russia's position.
The lawmakers pledged to continue pressing for answers and accountability.
The dispute has renewed questions about Ukraine's dependence on a single private company for critical military communications.
Retired US Army Lieutenant Colonel Amos Fox, a fellow at Arizona State University's Future Security Initiative, told RFE/RL that the situation illustrates the risks of relying on a single provider for essential military capabilities.
“A challenger to Musk’s dominance of this space would help insulate states like Ukraine from the political games of people like Musk,” Fox said.
A musician plays in a dark underpass in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv during a power outage on November 14 caused by Russian attacks on energy facilities in the country.
He also pointed to the influence that individuals outside government can exercise over national security decisions when states depend heavily on their companies and resources.
Paul Poast of the University of Chicago questioned whether the disruptions could be explained by technical problems alone.
While acknowledging that technology outages can occur, Poast told RFE/RL that he doubted the Starshield disruption was simply a glitch.
He noted Musk's previous comments that an earlier slowdown resulted from SpaceX's interpretation of its terms of service and questioned whether the latest disruptions could be connected to diplomatic efforts involving Ukraine and Russia.
Russia's Demands Are A Big Barrier To A Ukraine Peace Deal. What Are They?
Poast raised the possibility that the disruptions could have served as an indirect means of increasing pressure on Kyiv during negotiations, although he offered no evidence establishing such a connection.
The Starshield dispute comes as the Trump administration seeks to advance negotiations to end Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, with questions over territorial concessions and European security remaining contentious.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner -- Trump's son-in-law -- said they remained in contact with Moscow, Kyiv, and European partners following trilateral discussions.
In a social media statement on November 14, Kushner said the next phase of negotiations would focus on facilitating direct engagement between Russia and European governments and preparing another round of trilateral talks.
He said several new ideas were being explored and stressed that any eventual agreement must include credible security guarantees for Ukraine.
“President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine’s and Europe’s security and make future conflict less likely,” Kushner wrote.
His comments followed criticism from Republican Senator Tom Cotton, who rejected reported Russian demands that NATO withdraw forces from Eastern Europe.
“NATO nations withdrawing from their own borders is a preposterous demand by Russia,” Cotton said, adding that Moscow would stop fighting only when it understood it could not win.
European leaders have also warned against pressuring Kyiv into territorial concessions.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on November 14 that countries seeking to limit assistance to Ukraine were effectively trying to impose an unjust peace, warning that such an approach could lead to another war.
The White House and Pentagon had not responded to requests for comment on the latest Starshield disruptions as of late November 14.

Fed Rate Hikes Threaten U.S. Farm Margins as Debt Hits $605 Billion
The Fed signals more rate hikes as U.S. farm debt nears $605 billion, raising concerns over credit costs, shrinking margins and 2027 planting decisions.
Marcus Ellington is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural markets, global trade, and agricultural policy, with an international perspective on their impact across the global agri-food system.
Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins supported gradual interest rate increases on November 14, 2026 , citing persistent inflation and economic uncertainty. Her remarks, reported by Reuters, come as U.S. agriculture faces rising debt, elevated production costs and tighter operating margins. With the USDA projecting $605.1 billion in total farm debt for 2026 , additional monetary tightening could increase financing expenses just as producers prepare their 2027 planting budgets and investment decisions.
The Federal Reserve's benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75% to 4% , with markets anticipating another quarter-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting. Collins favors smaller, measured adjustments rather than aggressive tightening, although she acknowledged that economic data could change the policy outlook. For farmers, higher rates can translate into more expensive operating loans, machinery financing and farmland purchases, particularly for operations relying on variable-rate credit.
Bacteria and Fungi Boost Crop Yields by Nearly 15%, Analysis of 172 Studies Finds
Farm Debt and Input Costs Add Pressure to Agricultural Margins
According to the USDA Economic Research Service's September 2026 forecast, U.S. farm debt is expected to rise 4.6% to $605.1 billion , while production expenses could reach $492.8 billion, an increase of 4.5% . Net farm income is projected at $158.4 billion, down 2.6% in nominal terms. These figures highlight the financial pressure facing producers, although conditions vary considerably by commodity, region and farm size. Higher interest expenses could further reduce cash flow for operations already managing narrow margins.
Input inflation is adding another challenge. USDA projections indicate that spending on fertilizers, lime and soil conditioners could increase 15.3% in 2026 , while fuel and oil expenses may rise 28.8%. For corn, soybean and wheat producers, these increases complicate decisions about fertilizer purchases, equipment upgrades and acreage allocation. Agricultural cooperatives and input suppliers may also face higher working-capital costs, potentially influencing pricing, inventory management and financing terms offered to farmers.
The effect of higher rates depends on individual loan agreements. For example, a producer carrying $500,000 in variable-rate debt would pay approximately $1,250 more annually if the applicable interest rate increased by 0.25 percentage points and the outstanding balance remained unchanged. A half-point increase would add roughly $2,500. Actual borrowing costs depend on lender pricing, repayment schedules and loan structure, meaning Federal Reserve decisions do not automatically produce equivalent increases in agricultural loan rates.
Monetary tightening could also influence agricultural commodity markets. Higher U.S. interest rates may strengthen the dollar, making American corn, soybeans and wheat less competitive in some export markets. However, exchange rates are only one factor affecting commodity prices. Global crop yields, weather conditions, trade policies and international demand remain critical. For livestock producers, more expensive financing could affect herd expansion, feed purchases and investments in facilities, particularly when operating costs are already elevated.
December Fed Decision Raises Questions for 2027 Farm Financing
The Federal Reserve's December meeting will provide an important signal for agricultural lenders and producers preparing next year's budgets. Reuters reported that Collins considers gradual tightening appropriate because inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target , while higher long-term borrowing costs may already be restraining economic activity. The pace and extent of additional increases remain uncertain, with policymakers weighing persistent inflation against the risk of weakening economic growth.
Farmers entering the 2027 production cycle face decisions involving credit renewals, machinery purchases, fertilizer commitments and crop marketing. Variable-rate debt exposure, liquidity and debt-service costs are becoming increasingly relevant to those calculations. USDA Farm Service Agency lending programs, Farm Credit System institutions and crop insurance can support financial planning, although their availability and protection vary. For highly leveraged operations, even modest changes in financing costs may influence planting decisions and investment schedules.

items.title: A Larger-Than-Normal Fed Rate Hike in December Now Looks More Likely. Here's Why. - The Motley Fool
items.summary: A Larger-Than-Normal Fed Rate Hike in December Now Looks More Likely. Here's Why.  The Motley Fool
items.content:
One Federal Reserve official says a larger rate hike in December is appropriate.
The personal consumption expenditure price index on Nov. 25 will be critical.
When it raises interest rates to fight inflation, the Federal Reserve typically moves very gradually, hiking its target rate by a quarter of a percentage point at a time.
But December may be different. That's because, after raising the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point at its September meeting, the Fed's monetary policy committee paused in October to see if inflation was beginning to cool.
Suddenly, it looks like that was a poor decision. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), the main measure of inflation in the U.S., was just published and showed that inflation was higher than expected in October. The overall price level rose 0.4% month over month, higher than the 0.3% expected and well above the 0.2% level the Fed would like to see.
Higher energy prices, related to the ongoing conflict with Iran, continued to add to overall inflation. But other sectors saw larger-than-expected increases, too, including housing.
As a result, the Fed may have to play catch-up at its last meeting of the year, on Dec. 8-9. That means it could move from its typical quarter-point hike to a half-point hike, which could be jarring for financial markets unused to larger rate increases .
In fact, one Fed official said it out loud. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Nov. 10 in a speech in London that a 50-basis-point (bp) hike -- equivalent to half of a percentage point -- is merited. If October's core CPI rate (the rate that excludes volatile food and fuel costs) came in at 0.3% or higher, he said, "I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting." And indeed, core CPI in October was 0.3%.
It's not yet clear that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is on board with a 50 bp hike in December, and we may get little indication of how he's leaning before that meeting, as he has come out against giving markets hints of what he's thinking.
But I think he'll be won over to a larger hike. Despite not hiking the federal funds rate in October, Warsh sounded very hawkish at his press conference after the October meeting, and with the economy and the labor market appearing very healthy at the moment, he may reason that a larger rate hike won't harm them much.
Right now, futures traders are pricing in an 87% chance of a quarter-point hike and a 13% chance of a half-point hike. But I believe that will change in the coming weeks. The next key data point to watch is the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, which will be published on Nov. 25.
If that index, like the CPI, comes in hotter than expected, I expect a half-point hike in December.

items.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
items.summary: Front-runner Carmelle emerges victorious with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra.
items.content:
Figure caption, Philippines' Carmelle has won the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra
By Jonathan Head ,Â  South East Asia correspondent, in Bangkok ,Â  Thuong Le ,Â  Reporting from Bangkok Â  and Â  Jack Grey ,Â  BBC News
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.
Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.
She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.
There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.
Image caption, Carmelle was the youngest contestant in the competition at 19 years old
Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.
Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.
Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.
And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.
However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.
Image caption, Thinla wore a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit during her performance
The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.
Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.
Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.
Image caption, Vietnam's Toc Tien came third with 164 points
Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.
There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.
Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.
Image caption, Eurvosion superfans Michael, Scarlett and Zelie travelled from the UK to Thailand to watch Eurovision Asia's first outing
Korea, Vietnam and Laos also received praise from Pereira and her friends Michael Peters and Scarlett Massie, both from England.
"It was amazing, a very high standard," said Massie.
"The dance was amazing. The sets were amazing. The costumes were amazing. The singing was amazing. Incredible", Peters added.
They confidently declared that "Asia Vision" should be the name for next year's show.
For some, it seems the excitement for another edition is already building.
However the crowd at the One Bangkok Arena thinned out not long after the Philippines singer Carmelle lifted the trophy.
The arena was crowded, but not full, and it's still not clear how much commitment there is among regional broadcasters to keep the contest going and expand it to more than 11 countries.

UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars
Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais .
In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.
Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.
New airport style drive-in biometrics kiosks at Eurotunnel in Calais. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.
In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.
The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France , have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.
The new drive-in fingerprinting terminals at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.
Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.
Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.
Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.
The new drive-in border controls at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.
Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question we are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

Rep. Thomas Massie says he will force a vote to end U.S. involvement in Iran war
LOUISVILLE, Ky. — Kentucky Congressman Thomas Massie says he plans to force a vote in the U.S. House of Representatives on whether to pull troops out of hostilities with Iran before he leaves office.
Video in player above: Rep. Thomas Massie to force second vote on Epstein files
On Saturday, Massie announced that he had introduced a resolution earlier in the week directing President Donald Trump to remove U.S. armed forces from the war with Iran.
The resolution, H.Con.Res. 126, invokes the War Powers Resolution, a federal law that gives Congress a say in whether the military gets involved in foreign conflicts.
Massie said he could force a vote on his resolution in mid-December if House Speaker Mike Johnson does not cancel any scheduled legislative days.
House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
He also said two other Iran-related War Powers resolutions, H.Con.Res. 86 and H.Con.Res. 89, are already waiting for action in the House and could come up for a vote before his.
Massie said he intends to ensure a vote takes place before his term ends at the beginning of next year.
"I'll be forcing a vote to END THE WAR in Iran before my term is up," Massie wrote.
The resolution would direct the president to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran.
It does not, by itself, guarantee an end to the war or require other countries to stop their involvement.

items.title: Thomas Massie Offers Republicans a 'Life Boat From MAGA' Over Iran War - Newsweek
items.summary: Thomas Massie Offers Republicans a 'Life Boat From MAGA' Over Iran War  Newsweek
items.content:
See more of our trusted coverage when you search. Prefer Newsweek on Google to see more of our trusted coverage when you search.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie says he is offering his colleagues a "life boat from MAGA" as he prepares another attempt to force a congressional vote on ending President Donald Trump 's war in Iran .
The Kentucky congressman, who will leave office in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, said he is trying to persuade more Republicans to break with the president over the conflict.
"I'm offering Republicans a life boat from MAGA," Massie told Fox News Digital in an interview published Saturday.
He also accused Republicans of remaining "still in the suicide pact with this administration," suggesting that continued loyalty to Trump could carry political consequences following the GOP's losses in the November 3 midterm elections.
Massie later wrote on X: "I'll be forcing a vote to END THE WAR in Iran before my term is up."
The effort could force Republican lawmakers to take another public position on the conflict before Democrats assume control of Congress in January. But whether Massie can attract enough additional GOP support remains uncertain.
Newsweek reached out to Massie and the White House on Saturday.
Thomas Massie Seeks Republican Defectors Over Iran War
Massie told Fox that another War Powers resolution could reach the House floor in the "next few legislative days" or around Christmas.
The measure would seek to direct the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities in Iran, challenging the Trump administration's authority to continue military operations without congressional authorization.
Massie has been seeking additional Republican support, although lawmakers interviewed by Fox offered differing assessments of his prospects.
Representative Jeff Van Drew, a New Jersey Republican, told Fox that "one or two" additional Republicans could support the measure.
Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, who previously supported an Iran War Powers resolution, told Fox on Thursday that he would maintain his position if the new measure resembled the previous legislation.
Barrett, however, expressed skepticism that significantly more Republicans would break ranks.
House Armed Services Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, an Alabama Republican, said he would oppose the resolution but confirmed that Massie had been speaking with colleagues.
"Massie has been having conversations with members," Rogers told Fox.
Barrett, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania were among seven Republicans who joined Democrats in passing an Iran War Powers resolution in September. The measure passed the House 220-204.
Massie's latest effort would revisit that fight following Republicans' midterm losses, with the Kentucky congressman hoping to persuade more members of his party to break with Trump. The previous House vote did not compel the administration to withdraw U.S. forces, underscoring the obstacles facing another attempt to end the war through Congress.
Iran War Exposes Republican Divisions After Midterms
Massie's appeal comes less than two weeks after Republicans suffered major losses in the midterm elections, with the Iran war emerging as a source of internal disagreement over the party's direction.
Vice President JD Vance acknowledged the war's political consequences following the election, writing on X: "The reason we lost is the war."
Massie has made a similar argument, suggesting that Republicans who continue supporting the conflict risk further alienating voters.
At a November 9 news conference, Massie argued that the war's economic consequences were particularly damaging to the party.
"People are more opposed to the consequences of this war than they are this war," he said, pointing to rising gasoline and diesel prices, fertilizer costs and grocery bills.
He also urged Republicans to distance themselves from the administration's handling of the conflict.
"This is the best vote you can take right now to put some daylight between yourself and the failed policy of this war in Iran. And the way that it's been handled," Massie said.
Polling suggests that opposition to continuing the war extends into the Republican electorate.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted November 6-9 found that 51 percent of Republicans supported Congress passing legislation to end the Iran war.
Democrats, meanwhile, believe the election results could encourage additional Republicans to challenge Trump.
"The threat of Trump dumping a lot of money into Republican districts is over, perhaps more members of Congress we think represent their communities will listen to what constituents are saying about the war," Democratic Representative Adelita Grijalva of Arizona told Fox.
Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts also expressed hope that Republicans would change their positions.
"If they're listening to the people that sent them here, yes," she told the outlet.
Massie's latest challenge follows months of clashes with Trump over the Iran war, government spending and the release of files relating to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The libertarian-leaning Republican has repeatedly argued that Trump's military operations in Iran contradict the "America First" promises that helped bring him back to the White House.
In August, Massie warned that the conflict could become the administration's "biggest and most costly blunder."
He cited military spending, higher costs for consumers and damage to America's international standing.
"We should walk away from this now," Massie wrote at the time.
Trump backed former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein in his successful May primary challenge against Massie, ensuring the congressman's nearly 14-year tenure representing Kentucky's 4th Congressional District would end in January.
The president has repeatedly portrayed Massie as disloyal to the Republican Party. Earlier this week, Trump called him a "stone-cold loser" while defending Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth against Massie's impeachment effort.
Massie has also challenged Trump over the Epstein files. On Wednesday, he announced that a discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had secured the 218 signatures needed to advance the measure toward a House vote. The effort drew support from Democrats and several other Republicans, including Fitzpatrick, Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman.
Pete Hegseth Impeachment Vote Adds to Pressure Over Iran War
Massie's renewed War Powers push also follows his unsuccessful attempt to advance eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth.
Three of the articles accused the defense secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 through the administration's military operations against Iran.
Other allegations concerned civilian casualties, military operations in Venezuela and Yemen, strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels, and alleged retaliation against Democratic Senator Mark Kelly.
The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, blocking immediate consideration of the charges without holding a vote on whether Hegseth should be impeached. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans did not vote.
Trump celebrated the result, declaring that Hegseth had been exonerated.
Hegseth also rejected the allegations, calling the impeachment effort a political "farce" and accusing Massie of undermining American military personnel .
"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," Hegseth said during a Pentagon news conference.
Massie has maintained that his objections concern constitutional limits on presidential war powers rather than a personal disagreement with the defense secretary.
Unlike the impeachment effort, the proposed War Powers resolution would directly address whether U.S. forces should remain engaged in hostilities in Iran.
Massie has pledged to force a vote before his congressional term expires in January, although a specific date has not been announced.
The War Powers Resolution of 1973 establishes procedures intended to preserve Congress's constitutional role in decisions involving military conflict. However, the administration has not withdrawn U.S. forces following previous House votes seeking to curtail the war.
A concurrent resolution does not require the president's signature, but whether it can legally compel the withdrawal of U.S. forces is disputed. Binding legislation directing an end to the conflict could also face a presidential veto.
Trump and his administration have defended the Iran campaign as necessary to counter threats from Tehran, while Massie and other critics argue that sustained hostilities require congressional authorization.
Massie will leave Congress in January, when Gallrein succeeds him and Democrats take control of the House.
Before then, his proposed vote could establish whether opposition to Trump's Iran policy is spreading among House Republicans—or remains largely confined to lawmakers who have already broken with the president.

Warren Buffett Issued His Starkest Warning About the Stock Market in Years. Here's What History Says Comes Next.
There's been no shortage of market volatility over the last week. After experiencing their worst week of 2026 in early November, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) are rallying once again.
However, that doesn't mean that investors are in the clear. The tech industry is still struggling with volatility -- especially after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's recent ousting -- and the market is the priciest it's been in decades.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Warren Buffett has also issued a direct warning to investors who may be underestimating market risk right now, and history has both good and bad news about what's coming next.
During Berkshire Hathaway 's 2026 meeting, Buffett discussed his thoughts on the current market in an interview with CNBC. He warned that in this historically expensive market, some investors are taking on too much risk.
"I've compared the markets to a church with a casino attached," he noted, with the church representing fundamentals-based long-term investing and the casino depicting short-term buying.
[T]he casino has gotten very attractive to people," Buffett warned, adding, "that's not investing, it's not speculating, it's gambling." He emphasized, however, that "that doesn't mean that investing is terrible. It does mean that prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly."
The S&P 500 has notched more than two dozen record highs so far in 2026, but the downside to all of that growth is that some stocks are at risk of becoming overvalued.
The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE Ratio measures the S&P 500's valuation over time based on its 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings. The higher the metric climbs, the more likely the index is overvalued and due for a pullback.
While no market indicator can predict when recessions or bear markets will begin, this particular metric has a long track record of preceding downturns. In 1929, for example, it spiked just before the Great Depression began. It surged again in 1999, during the dot-com bubble. Most recently, it peaked in late 2021, just months before stocks sank into a bear market.
In 2026, this metric reached its highest level since the dot-com bubble burst -- surpassing 40 for only the second time in stock market history. While this doesn't necessarily mean a crash is imminent, it does mean the market is incredibly richly valued right now.
The market may be pricey, but that doesn't mean it's a bad time to buy. It's crucial, however, to maintain a long-term outlook.
As Buffett mentioned, not all investing is bad. While some stocks may be overvalued right now, there are still plenty of fairly priced and even undervalued stocks with plenty of room for growth.
History also proves time and again that quality stocks will thrive over time. Since 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has faced the dot-com bubble, the Great Recession, the COVID-19 crash, the 2022 bear market, and countless smaller corrections along the way. It's also up by nearly 750% in that time.
It's impossible to say where the market is headed in the near term. But if history has just one lesson for investors, it's that healthy stocks and a long-term outlook are the keys to surviving whatever volatility may be looming.

items.content:
But inflation for the month came in higher than expected.
Wednesday, Nov. 25, is shaping up to be a big day for the stock market.
That morning, an hour before the opening bell on Wall Street, the Bureau of Economic Analysis is scheduled to release the Personal Income and Outlays report for October.
The monthly report contains valuable data on Americans' disposable income and spending , providing a picture of the health of consumer finances, which drives the economy. But more importantly, the report includes the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's favored measure of inflation in the U.S. economy.
That index is always important, but I would argue that the October report is particularly critical, as the Fed now stands at a crossroads on interest rate hikes. The PCE index will likely be the deciding data point.
The Fed hiked its target interest rate in September but then paused at its October monetary policy meeting to await additional information on inflation.
In retrospect, that looks like a bad decision. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), a critical measure of inflation in the U.S., was recently published and showed that inflation was higher than expected in October. The overall price level rose 0.4% month over month, higher than the 0.3% expected and well above the 0.2% level the Fed would like to see.
So the Fed is now kind of behind the eight ball, and it may need to play catch-up at its upcoming Dec. 8-9 meeting. It's starting to look like that means it will raise its target rate by a half-percentage point at that meeting, rather than the typical quarter-point hike.
One Fed governor, Christopher Waller, already said as much. If core CPI (which excludes volatile food and fuel prices) for October hits 3% or higher, he said a half-point rate increase is appropriate in December. And that's what happened.
I think the rest of the Fed's monetary policy committee will be watching the Nov. 25 PCE price index and, if it too comes in higher than expected (as CPI did), will also embrace a half-point hike.
Such a large rate hike is uncommon for the Fed, which typically moves in quarter-point increments. It's unclear how the stock market will respond to such a move by the central bank, but I don't think it will be positive.
That's why I'll be watching that Nov. 25 PCE report. It will be the last measure of inflation before the Fed's December meeting and may well decide if the Fed has to take dramatic action then.
