items.title: How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts
items.summary: ETF experts say Nvidia’s leadership turmoil and Democratic control of Congress could shift AI demand to the benefit of other Big Tech stocks, rival chipmakers.
items.content:
Nvidia AI trade: Huang exit, Congress reshape Big Tech stock outlook
Despite new headline risks, Big Tech may keep getting bigger, say ETF experts
The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's " ETF Edge " earlier this week.
"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF ( MAGS ).
Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.
"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.
Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF ( NCLD ) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."
The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.
CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.
Performance of the Roundhill Neocloud ETF year to date in 2026.
Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.
Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF ( IVES ) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.
AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.
Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.
"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."
The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.
Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.
"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

The Bank of England next meets on 17 December to decide whether to increase the cost of borrowing. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
The Bank of England next meets on 17 December to decide whether to increase the cost of borrowing. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and UK households are expected to pick up the tab
Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy
A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.
A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.
So sclerotic is the economy, so lacking in flexibility or productive spare capacity, that even the burst of growth experienced by the UK over the last year, defying most forecasters, must be calmed down with higher interest rates or else inflation will rip.
Huw Pill, the Bank’s chief economist, told the Financial Times on Saturday that more than one rate rise was almost certain .
This is not a message anyone who borrows money will want to hear, especially when the festive season is in full swing. If interest rates edge up from 4% to 4.25%, mortgage deals will rise and business loans will become more expensive.
The central bank expects businesses to react to the higher costs of doing business by hitting their customers with price hikes. It is an argument that presumes consumers have money available to pay higher prices, despite plenty of evidence to the contrary. Only households in the top half of the income scale have spent more this year and that has depended on running down their savings.
Consumers are also battle-hardened after the greedflation period following the pandemic that morphed into its evil cousin, shrinkflation. They know about grifting retailers and consumer product suppliers that try to build a narrative about the inevitability of surging inflation to disguise their own price hikes.
Christmas lights on Oxford Street, London. Will consumers be prepared to pay higher prices, or have the spare cash to do so? Photograph: Jack Hall/PA The Bank says its business surveys have failed to detect efforts by the corporate sector to increase prices. It’s just that a majority of policymakers are convinced pressure is building and inflation will be more than double their 2% target in a few months.
But if consumers don’t have any spare cash, or have become more savvy about how they spend it, there is still a weak link – a special kind of consumer who could aid corporates in pushing up prices.
The weak link is the state, or government in all its forms. The NHS is a big purchaser, so is local government and the many agencies that are funded by government, from Homes England to National Highways. Government expenditure on goods and services accounts for 25% of overall consumption in the economy.
Everything from concrete and medical supplies to food and furniture will cost more, and sellers will be prepared to justify the rise with a wide range of excuses.
Corporates will blame the war in the Middle East for an increase in transport costs and the impact of climate change that makes growing stuff harder. They will even accuse the government of raising costs by introducing new worker protection rules.
Let’s add another one: contractors will say they can’t get the skilled staff and so must pass on the cost of higher wages.
After 15 years of austerity and job cuts, there is a question mark over whether the public sector has the nous and resolve to push back to keep costs in check.
Budgets on the London to Birmingham high-speed rail line (HS2) have spiralled out of control. The costs of the next largest infrastructure project in England, the 14.5-mile (23km) lower Thames crossing linking Essex and Kent via two tunnels, have more than doubled to £11bn.
Budgets on HS2 have spiralled out of control. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Government spending on consultants reached £3.7bn in 2024-25 from £2.9bn in 2022-23 and there seems to be no end to their uses, from advisers on artificial intelligence to strategies for reaching net zero.
The public sector is also notorious for commissioning plans for new town or city developments for which there is no funding, except for the inflationary bill from consultants.
These public sector organisations have huge clout, and should use it. If they do, there will be knock-on effects to inflation deals struck within the business community, which in many cases can only ramp up prices knowing the public sector is the ultimate buyer.
Inside Threadneedle Street, policymakers expect everyone – consumers, government and business – to cave in to sellers’ demands. And that many of the UK’s 33 million workers will subsequently demand big pay rises to compensate.
Yet it must be possible that all three consumer groups will adopt the slogan Can’t Pay, Won’t Pay, limiting the rise in inflation and eliminating the need for elevated pay rises.
Even if the poor, financially bombed-out household consumer is the only one to take a stand against greedy corporates, inflation will not hit the heights forecast by the Bank of England. In the meantime, it might have raised interest rates too far, laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy.

items.title: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips - CNN
items.summary: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips  CNN
items.content:
Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.
In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.
But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia , the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.
At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.
Also known as Huang Le , the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.
But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.
“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”
But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.
On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.
“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.
The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026.
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.
US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.
Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.
Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.
“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”
The orange Alibaba logo is displayed on the sunlit glass facade of the Shenzhen Alibaba Center on November 11, in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China.
Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.
In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.
Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.
“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.
“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.
In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.
A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.
Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.
Eric and Lara Trump, SpaceX, Twitter and electric car maker Tesla CEO Elon Musk (C), US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth and Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang walk off Air Force One upon arriving at Beijing Capital Airport in Beijing on May 13.
However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.
They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”
Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.
Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.
Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.
A growing number of chip smuggling cases has fueled calls for harsher legal enforcement outside the US as well. The Taiwanese government is seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong.
“There’s going to have to be new standards that are going to have to be enforced around traceability and transparency,” Capri said. “This is really going to be the beginning of a major crackdown, and actually moving on to the next phase of export control enforcement.”
CNN’s Yong Xiong, Isaac Yee and Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

Nvidia CEO Departure Prompts Lynx Equity Analyst to Reassess AI Semiconductor Growth Risks
Nvidia on phone ©Adobe Stock Images Nvidia's (NASDAQ:NVDA) leadership upheaval could have implications for the wider artificial intelligence semiconductor industry, according to KC Rajkumar of Lynx Equity Strategies, who has adopted a more cautious position on the sector despite previously expressing a positive outlook.
In a research note titled "AI Semis: The Calm Before the Storm," Rajkumar warned that uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's financial relationships and the future of US semiconductor export controls could lead to revisions in industry earnings forecasts.
The analyst suggested that investors may not yet have fully assessed the potential consequences for companies supplying processors, equipment and infrastructure to the AI market.
Leadership Transition Brings Nvidia's Business Relationships Into Focus
Nvidia announced the immediate resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang on November 12.
The departure followed reports about alleged personal relationships, including claims involving Alice Huang, a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while beginning the process of selecting a permanent successor.
The developments have increased scrutiny of the company's China operations, customer relationships and financial arrangements supporting AI infrastructure projects.
Rajkumar believes the relatively restrained reaction across other semiconductor stocks may reflect uncertainty about the implications rather than confidence that the risks have been fully accounted for.
AI Infrastructure Financing Could Influence Chip Demand
The analyst identified financing relationships within the AI industry as a potential source of wider market risk.
Nvidia's investments and financial arrangements with companies participating in AI infrastructure development have helped support demand for its processors, according to Rajkumar's assessment.
If these arrangements are reduced or projects lose funding, demand for semiconductors and related infrastructure equipment could be affected.
The potential consequences would not necessarily be limited to Nvidia.
Other chipmakers, equipment suppliers and companies involved in AI infrastructure development could also experience changes in customer demand.
Rajkumar raised the possibility that a reduction in financing activity could prompt companies to reassess their revenue and earnings assumptions.
However, no industry-wide wave of project cancellations has been established.
Rajkumar suggested that semiconductor companies may need to review their financial expectations for 2027 as the implications of Nvidia's leadership change become clearer.
The analyst said investors appeared uncertain about where potential earnings reductions might emerge across the supply chain.
Upcoming investor conferences could provide additional information about AI spending plans, project financing and customer demand.
Such disclosures may help determine whether existing earnings estimates remain appropriate.
The uncertainty has contributed to Rajkumar's decision to maintain a defensive position on AI-related semiconductor equities.
Commerce Department Scrutiny Creates Additional Policy Risk
The Nvidia developments have coincided with questions about the enforcement of US restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced scrutiny over the administration's approach to companies suspected of diverting restricted processors to Chinese customers.
Axios reported on November 11 that Lutnick had resisted efforts by other administration officials to strengthen enforcement.
Reuters reported the following day that senior White House officials were discussing whether he should be removed.
Lawmakers from both parties have also called for greater scrutiny of the Commerce Department's enforcement practices.
These reports have raised questions about whether US semiconductor export policy could become more restrictive.
Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, has become part of the discussion surrounding semiconductor export enforcement.
Alice Huang, an executive associated with the company, has reportedly been suspected by US intelligence officials of having connections to Chinese intelligence.
Those suspicions have not been established as fact, and the reports do not demonstrate wrongdoing by the individuals or companies involved.
Nevertheless, the allegations have contributed to scrutiny of how US authorities monitor the movement of advanced semiconductor technology.
Rajkumar warned that a change in Commerce Department leadership or export policy could have significant implications for the industry.
He suggested that tighter restrictions could extend beyond Nvidia's AI processors to a broader range of US semiconductor products.
China Export Restrictions Could Compound Demand Risks
A more restrictive US export policy could affect American semiconductor companies' ability to serve customers in China.
Rajkumar identified this possibility as a separate risk that could coincide with weaker AI infrastructure spending.
If both developments occurred, semiconductor companies could face reduced demand alongside limitations on access to an important international market.
The combined effects could influence earnings projections for 2027.
The potential restrictions remain uncertain, and the report does not establish that broader export controls have been introduced.
However, the possibility contributes to the analyst's concerns about the visibility of future semiconductor revenue.
Attractive Valuations May Not Offset Earnings Uncertainty
Rajkumar acknowledged that some semiconductor stocks are trading at valuations he considers attractive.
Even so, he expressed doubts about whether investors would be prepared to increase their holdings while earnings forecasts remain uncertain.
The analyst's concern is that current estimates may not fully reflect potential reductions in AI investment or changes to export regulations.
A downward revision to expected earnings could alter how investors assess existing share prices.
Rajkumar therefore indicated that he would prefer to wait for additional information before becoming more constructive on the sector.

items.content:
Nvidia Leadership Crisis Raises Concerns Over AI Semiconductor Earnings and US Export Restrictions
The leadership crisis at Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has prompted concerns about the wider semiconductor industry, with Lynx Equity Strategies analyst KC Rajkumar warning that uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence investment and US export policies could affect earnings expectations across the sector.
In a research note titled "AI Semis: The Calm Before the Storm," Rajkumar suggested that investors were struggling to assess the potential consequences of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's sudden departure and its implications for companies involved in the AI supply chain.
The analyst, who has previously maintained a positive outlook on AI-related semiconductor stocks, indicated that the developments could lead to a broader reassessment of industry growth forecasts, particularly for 2027.
Nvidia CEO Departure Creates Uncertainty Across AI Supply Chain
Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12 with immediate effect, following media reports concerning alleged personal relationships.
The reports included allegations involving Alice Huang, a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by US authorities of having connections to Chinese intelligence. Those suspicions have not been established as fact.
Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim chief executive and initiated a search for a permanent replacement.
The leadership change has brought additional attention to Nvidia's business activities in China, its relationships with customers and partners, and the financial arrangements supporting investment in AI infrastructure.
Rajkumar said the relatively limited reaction among other semiconductor stocks should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that investors have fully assessed the potential consequences.
Instead, he suggested that uncertainty about the scale and distribution of possible financial effects may be preventing investors from making substantial changes to their earnings forecasts.
A central concern identified by Rajkumar involves financing arrangements between Nvidia and other participants in the artificial intelligence industry.
Some of these arrangements involve investments and financial relationships among companies that develop, purchase or operate AI infrastructure.
The analyst warned that a reduction in such financing could affect demand for Nvidia's processors and other equipment used in AI data centres.
If projects lose financial backing or existing arrangements are reduced, the effects could extend beyond Nvidia to other semiconductor manufacturers and infrastructure providers.
Rajkumar raised the possibility that cancellations or reductions in AI-related projects could require companies to revise their expected revenue and earnings.
However, the report did not establish that a widespread wave of project cancellations had occurred.
The concerns therefore relate to potential developments rather than confirmed reductions in industry demand.
Semiconductor Earnings Forecasts for 2027 Could Be Revised
Rajkumar believes the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia could have implications for semiconductor companies' financial projections for 2027.
The analyst suggested that investors may be reluctant to adjust earnings estimates until they have greater clarity about the extent of Nvidia's financial relationships across the AI industry.
He expects upcoming investor conferences to provide additional information about company spending plans, customer demand and potential changes to existing arrangements.
The resulting disclosures could influence how analysts assess future revenue growth and profitability across the semiconductor supply chain.
Rajkumar's concerns centre on whether current earnings expectations adequately reflect the possibility of reduced AI infrastructure investment.
US Export Controls Add Another Source of Uncertainty
The developments at Nvidia have coincided with renewed scrutiny of US semiconductor export policies and the role of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
According to an Axios report published on November 11, Lutnick had resisted efforts by other administration officials to strengthen enforcement against companies suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia processors to China.
Reuters subsequently reported on November 12 that senior White House officials were discussing whether Lutnick should be removed from his position.
Lawmakers from both major US political parties have also called for greater examination of the Commerce Department's enforcement of semiconductor export restrictions.
These developments have introduced uncertainty about the future direction of US policy governing advanced chip sales to China.
Megaspeed Links Nvidia Controversy to Export Enforcement
Part of the scrutiny concerns Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia.
Alice Huang, an executive associated with Megaspeed, has reportedly been suspected by US intelligence officials of having connections to Chinese intelligence.
The allegations remain unproven, and the existence of such suspicions does not establish wrongdoing by Huang or Megaspeed.
The controversy has nevertheless drawn attention to questions about how US authorities monitor semiconductor exports and investigate potential attempts to circumvent restrictions.
Rajkumar warned that a change in leadership at the Commerce Department, or a reversal of existing policies, could have consequences for semiconductor companies.
He suggested that a more restrictive approach might extend beyond Nvidia's advanced AI processors to additional US semiconductor products.
Tighter China Restrictions Could Affect Industry Revenue
China remains an important market for semiconductor companies, making potential changes to US export regulations relevant to future revenue expectations.
Rajkumar identified the possibility of broader restrictions as another risk to the sector's financial outlook.
If US authorities introduce additional limitations on semiconductor exports, American chipmakers could face reduced access to Chinese customers.
Such measures could affect revenue projections for 2027, particularly if they coincide with slower investment in AI infrastructure.
The analyst suggested that the combined effects of weaker demand and tighter export controls could be more significant than either development considered separately.
However, broader restrictions remain a potential policy outcome rather than an established change.
Lower Semiconductor Valuations May Not Prompt Immediate Buying
Rajkumar acknowledged that valuations across several semiconductor stocks have become more attractive following recent market developments.
Nevertheless, he questioned whether lower share prices would be sufficient to encourage investors to increase their exposure.
His concerns relate primarily to the reliability of future earnings forecasts rather than valuations in isolation.
If companies revise their AI growth expectations or encounter additional restrictions on sales to China, current earnings estimates may need to be adjusted.
This uncertainty could make investors reluctant to purchase semiconductor stocks despite lower valuations.
Rajkumar indicated that he would prefer greater clarity before adopting a more positive position on the sector.
Analyst Adopts Defensive Position on AI Semiconductor Stocks
The Lynx Equity Strategies analyst said he would like to become more constructive on AI-related semiconductor equities but intends to remain cautious in the near term.
He also indicated that he was positioning for the possibility of further declines as investors assess the consequences of Huang's departure.
The stance represents a change from his previously positive assessment of the semiconductor industry.
Rajkumar's analysis suggests that the implications of Nvidia's leadership transition may extend beyond the company's immediate operations.
Potential changes in AI financing, infrastructure spending and US export controls could influence earnings expectations across the industry.
The extent of those effects remains uncertain, with upcoming company disclosures and policy developments likely to provide additional information.

Israel fears surprise US strike on Iran as nuclear talks fuel concerns of escalation - analysis
To minimize risk of being caught off guard, the IDF is strengthening coordination with the US military and raising its level of alert across intelligence monitoring, early warning, and air defenses.
An Israeli Air Force fighter jet flies over central Israel amid the ongoing war between Israel, Iran and Hezbollah, March 12, 2026.
Ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran have put Israel's defense establishment on high alert over the possibility of being caught off guard by a sudden escalation.
Israeli security officials are preparing for three concerning scenarios: a surprise Iranian attack on US interests, including Israel; a sudden US decision to strike Iran without giving Israel sufficient advance warning; or a diplomatic agreement that would allow Tehran to resume uranium enrichment in the future, produce large quantities of precision ballistic missiles, and continue funding terrorist groups across the Middle East, including Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Houthis.
Such an agreement could allow Iran to maintain its position as the leading destabilizing force in the Middle East.
Tensions in the region are already running high. Iran's overnight attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain , carried out in retaliation for a strike on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps command and control facility, highlights the volatility of the situation and the extent to which American deterrence in the Middle East has weakened.
Sources within Israel's defense establishment acknowledge that US President Donald Trump's next moves are difficult to predict. US military officials have reportedly told their Israeli counterparts that they are preparing for the possibility of receiving orders to go from "zero to a hundred" at a moment's notice, allowing Washington to launch a surprise attack against Iran.
US Navy warships transit the Arabian Sea in close formation as CENTCOM forces continue to promote regional security and stability, June 30, 2026. (credit: US Navy photo)
"There were instances during the war when we were the ones updating them on what was happening," one Israeli security source said.
To reduce the risk of being caught off guard, the IDF is strengthening coordination with the US military and raising its alert level across intelligence monitoring, early warning, and air defense systems. The military is also maintaining its readiness to respond rapidly to any developments.
At the same time, Israel Air Force officials say regular assessments are being conducted to prevent fatigue among ground and air crews, many of whom have been operating under heightened alert for an extended period.
Concerns mount about Iran's proxy groups across the region
The security source said Israel is also considering a scenario in which critical intelligence received from foreign partners in the Middle East could prompt the country's political leadership to consider launching a preemptive strike.
Meanwhile, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir has visited the Lebanese border, where he warned Hezbollah and the Lebanese government that any involvement in an escalation led by Iran would be met with a severe military response.
Attention is now turning to the head of the IDF's Military Intelligence Directorate, Maj.-Gen. Shlomi Binder, as Israel's intelligence agencies work to identify potential threats and provide accurate early warnings.
The threats range from an isolated military incident to a coordinated campaign in which Iran and its regional proxies launch simultaneous attacks across the Middle East.
Israeli intelligence efforts are focused primarily on monitoring missile launchers and missile bases, amid assessments that Iran has restored approximately 20% of the ballistic missile production capacity it possessed before Operation Roaring Lion, following damage to its defense manufacturing facilities.
IDF officials believe the current tensions could continue for several weeks or even longer, raising concerns about the physical and operational strain on military personnel who have already spent an extended period on high alert.
To prevent fatigue from undermining operational readiness, the defense establishment is conducting regular situational assessments whenever new intelligence becomes available.

Anthropic’s S-1 Says Natural Gas, Not Chips, Is AI’s Biggest Bottleneck. Here’s the Stock That Sells the Engines.
Anthropic's S-1 filing revealed that power is still one of the biggest bottlenecks for artificial intelligence (AI) companies. For investors, that makes natural gas stocks particularly attractive, as Anthropic mentioned natural gas five times in just one paragraph in its filing.
There are a few ways to capitalize on that opportunity, ranging from owning shares of natural gas producers to owning shares of companies that own and operate pipelines and supply gas to data center campuses. One I'd lean toward is Energy Transfer (TXSE:ET), which operates over 140,000 miles of pipelines and associated energy infrastructure across 44 states.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
There's no publicly available information that Energy Transfer is connected to Anthropic. Rather, the bigger takeaway about natural gas from Anthropic's S-1 filing is how a company like Energy Transfer can benefit.
For example, certain of our planned data center facilities rely on dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation, which exposes us to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions outside our control, the costs of which we bear on a pass-through basis. These facilities are also subject to constraints on pipeline capacity and firm fuel transportation necessary to deliver natural gas.
Anthropic even notes that being unable to secure gas supply and transportation during facility development could cause "a planned site to be delayed or abandoned." That's a huge risk: not only to have a site delay when trying to create advanced AI models, but to potentially have to abandon a site completely. And that risk shows why access to natural gas is so important.
Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, which may go public in 2027, will win by having the best AI models. But Energy Transfer only needs AI use cases and adoption to increase to win, as it will create more power demand from AI companies. While the AI story is still in its early stages, it looks as if that's happening. According to research from The Motley Fool , 26.8% of U.S. businesses used AI in October 2026, compared with 3.7% in September 2023.
Energy Transfer is already capitalizing on that demand by signing an agreement with Oracle to supply natural gas to three of its data centers in the United States. It also has an agreement to provide a Nexus Data Center hyperscale campus with natural gas, as well as a 20-year binding agreement with Entergy Louisiana, a subsidiary of Entergy , to provide natural gas to its facilities in Louisiana. In a roundabout way, that connects Energy Transfer to Meta Platforms , as Meta is partnering with Entergy Louisiana to power a data center facility.
One of the biggest risks associated with Energy Transfer's AI opportunities is that building out pipelines and infrastructure could yield lower-than-expected returns.
Long-term debt is at $68.8 billion, a byproduct of building and expanding its extensive energy pipeline network. The debt is manageable as long as profits continue to grow, as we saw in the third quarter of 2026. For the third quarter, Energy Transfer's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) grew 31% from the prior-year period to $5 billion, which suggests the company's investments are paying off. But if debt keeps climbing while EBITDA falls, it's reasonable to question if the spending is justified.
With that understanding, there's still a lot to like about the company, including its 7% dividend yield and a dividend payout that has increased for 20 consecutive quarters. And as for where the stock price could head next, analysts are generally bullish. According to CNN-tracked data, of the 26 analysts who cover the stock, the median one-year price target is $25, representing a 28.6% gain from the Nov. 10 closing price of $19.43.

The bond market just turned on the AI trade — and chip stocks lost more than $650 billion in two days: Chart of the Day
Wall Street just had its best week since August, and chip stocks led the way. But by Friday the rally was cracking, and the bond market had turned against the AI trade.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) still finished the week up about 8%, with the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) up about 3.5% and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) up about 2.5%. Most of those gains came early. From Wednesday's close through Friday, a Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks lost more than $650 billion in market value, and only three rose.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) never joined the rally. The stock fell about 13% in the week Jensen Huang resigned as CEO , its worst week since April 2025 and its sixth straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2012. That wiped out about $570 billion in value as investors weighed Nvidia's $530 billion web of AI deals .
The damage spread to Nvidia's partners. Nebius ( NBIS ), in which Nvidia holds a stake, fell about 10% for the week after disappointing third quarter earnings . Nvidia-backed CoreWeave ( CRWV ) slid about 6% Friday, though it still finished up about 15% after strong quarterly results . Memory makers Micron ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ), leaders of the early-week bounce, gave back roughly 3% to 4% Friday.
The charts show where the rebound ran out of steam. The chip index stalled before it got back to its 200-day moving average , a long-term trend line. The Nasdaq-100 closed back below its own similar average, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) closed right at it.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index bounced off its Nov. 5 low near 9,000 but turned lower before reaching its 200-day average and the 11,100-11,200 zone that had held as a floor from May to October. · Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Bonds stopped breaking chips' fall
During the AI sell-off, Treasurys acted as a shock absorber. The 10-year yield ( ^TNX ) fell on all six of chip stocks' down days from Oct. 22 to Nov. 6, as investors bought bonds when chips sank.
But this past week, yields rose on all three days when semis were down. The 10-year jumped about 30 basis points to about 5.15%, and the 5-year climbed about 33 basis points. For both, it was the biggest weekly rise since April 2025.
On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller opened the door to a half-point rate hike , and hours later the October Consumer Price Index came in hot . On Friday, wholesale prices rose at their fastest annual pace in nearly four years .
Over the sell-off, every chip crash made traders doubt a hike was coming. Polymarket's odds of a Dec. 9 rate increase fell to about 66% after the Nov. 5 rout. By Friday, they were about 98%, with the odds of a half-point move up to 10%. Futures now price in about two quarter-point hikes by March 2027, up from one right after the crash.
Chips can't count on bonds to break their fall anymore.
Polymarket, Yahoo Finance There were still places to make money
The equal-weight S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ) has beaten the regular index by nearly 8 percentage points since the Oct. 6 record, the widest gap since May 2009.
Apple ( AAPL ), Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK-B ), where he remains the chair, and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) all closed at record highs Friday.
Next up is Nvidia's earnings report Tuesday after the close, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress . Investors will want to know whether the outlook holds without Huang.
Meanwhile, the bond market isn't waiting for that report. In a note on the views of its president, Jens Nordvig, Vanda Research summed up the new backdrop: "It's a different world, but arguably one with more opportunity."

Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has dismissed nine senior security officials over an alleged oil smuggling operation in the Jurf al-Nasr area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group.
Al-Zaidi chaired an emergency security meeting to review the findings of a committee investigating smuggling in Jurf al-Nasr, Babil province, military spokesperson Sabah al-Numan told the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The move follows an investigation that uncovered illegal oil refineries and evidence of manipulation linked to the smuggling activities.
“In light of the investigation’s findings, [the prime minister] ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary,” al-Numan said.
The prime minister “also ordered the dismissal” of nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil, he said.
The police chief of Babil province was among those dismissed.
Kataib Hezbollah, an Iran-aligned paramilitary group and one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, has recently issued several sharp statements against the prime minister, threatening his government and accusing him of corruption.
Senior Iraqi politicians previously told the AFP news agency that al-Zaidi had repeatedly said he was ready to confront groups refusing to disarm.
Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, said previous Iraqi governments had been careful not to address the issue of an alleged oil smuggling network worth up to $30m monthly.
“This area had effectively been run as a state within a state until now,” Smith said. “But that seems to have changed, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi saying that no inch of Iraq will be allowed to have oil smuggling operations like this.”
Two strategic oil pipelines running through the south of the country, just south of Baghdad, “had effectively been tapped into”, Smith said, citing a leaked intelligence report. “Oil was being siphoned off, stolen, and then sold on the black market in an operation worth tens of millions of dollars every month.”
On Wednesday, the INA reported that “intelligence documents” containing satellite images “showed crude oil and oil-derivatives smuggling operations carried out by an armed faction” in Jurf al-Nasr, accusing an unnamed group of tapping into a pipeline there.
Al-Numan said the investigating committee “confirmed the accuracy” of the information.
Akeel Abbas, a senior non-resident fellow at the Iraq Initiative within the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera that oil smuggling by various political factions and armed groups “is common in Iraq” due to “commercial rather than political or strategic” gains.
Abbas said the latest crackdown has more to do with “militia disarmament”.
“The prime minister cleverly decided to frame it as anticorruption. That is why a few days ago, there was a report leaked by the government about this operation,” he said.
The prime minister wants to “cut off the financial lifeline to this particular group that has been so resistant” to the government’s “militia disarmament” initiatives, he added.

A fter the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.
As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating , the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.
Chart showing how the past four years have overturned all monthly temperature records J anuary
A fire in Longwood, a town in Victoria, Australia, in early January. Photograph: Michael Currie/AAP Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia
As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average , Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.
People clear mud and debris outside homes in the aftermath of a storm, in Juiz de Fora, Brazil. Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPA Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain
The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month , triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.
Motorists drive through heavy rains in the Kibera slums in Nairobi, Kenya. Photograph: Donwilson Odhiambo/Getty Images Devastating floods across much of the world
In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water . Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.
The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO 2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.
A utility pole blocks a road in Saipan after a super typhoon with ferocious winds and relentless rains shredded tin roofs and forced people to take cover from flying tree limbs. Photograph: AP Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan
At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12 , leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.
A man seeks relief from the heat as temperatures rise in New Delhi, India. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia
At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat .
People assess the aftermath of landslides and flooding next to houses damaged in Attécoubé, a suburb of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. Photograph: Chris Boli/AFP/Getty Images Ocean heat enters uncharted territory
Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño , which is confirmed on 2 June.
Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth
Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June . Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.
Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo .
Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year , almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years .
Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup
Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.
At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.
Drone footage shows scale of destruction after Nepal floods – video
Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.
The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis . Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.
Typhoon Dujuan triggers deadly flooding and landslides in Japan – video
Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.
Protesters clash with police officers in Jakarta, Indonesia, during a demonstration against President Prabowo Subianto’s handling of forest fires. Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/Reuters Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño
The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.
Graph showing temperature anomalies in the Pacific Ocean Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires
Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade , which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.
After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.
Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels , curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.
Global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives. Photograph: Jesús Vargas/Getty Images 2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history
Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO 2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

NHS England on track to miss key cancer treatment target by 10,000 patients
Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership
Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.
The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.
Exclusive analysis of official figures for the Guardian reveals the NHS would have to treat 2,850 additional patients on time each month to get back on track, assuming patient volumes remain consistent.
According to calculations by Radiotherapy UK, 24,400 cancer patients a month would need to start treatment on time to hit the 80% target in March. But the NHS is only treating about 21,500 cancer patients a month within the 62-day target, leaving a monthly shortfall of 2,850 and a cumulative shortfall of 9,490 patients, the charity found.
Prof Pat Price, the chair of Radiotherapy UK and a leading oncologist, said: “The government is going to miss its cancer treatment target because the NHS does not have enough staff or equipment to treat the number of patients coming through its doors. This lack of leadership means thousands more people could die because they don’t get their treatment on time.”
A graph showing that NHS England is short of its target of treating 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referrals or consultant upgrade The analysis also found significant disparities between treatment of common cancer types. While more than two-thirds of patients with prostate and breast cancers were treated within two months ((70.1% and 68.8% respectively), only 60.9% of those with lung cancer and 60% of those with gynaecological cancers were treated on time. For head and neck cancers, barely half (56.5%) were. Regional inequalities were also stark, the research found. The Midlands had the lowest proportion treated on time, at 66.6%, compared with 77.3% in London.
Mark Lawler, a professor of digital health and chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, believes failures of accountability and focus are to blame. He said: “The whole system is being held together by goodwill glue alone. Lack of leadership is derailing efforts to improve cancer survival. Unless there is accountability for these failures by the NHS, a radical change in mindset and a focus on the basics, we will miss hitting treatment targets for another decade.”
The figures come as analysis of latest cancer diagnosis targets by Cancer Research UK shows that, over the last year, barely half (55.4%) of patients with cancer were diagnosed within 28 days of an urgent referral, against the faster diagnostic standard target of 80% , compared with 79.1% of patients who received the all-clear on time.
Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day
Naser Turabi, Cancer Research UK’s director of health policy and evidence, said hospital capacity was not able to keep pace with surging demand for cancer diagnosis – with urgent referrals in England up about 20% over the past four years alone. “While recent investment in diagnostic equipment is welcome, we’re not seeing enough progress to cut waiting times for the 6% of people who go on to receive a cancer diagnosis,” he said.
Dr Hilary Williams, the Royal College of Physicians clinical vice-president and a consultant in medical oncology, said crucial earlier diagnosis was only beneficial if patients could then be treated quickly.
“To close the gap, the NHS needs sufficient capacity across the whole cancer pathway,” Williams said. “That means more diagnostic capacity, including imaging, endoscopy and pathology, alongside the specialist workforce needed to deliver and interpret those tests. It also means enough treatment capacity in surgery, radiotherapy and systemic treatments so that diagnosing people more quickly doesn’t simply move the bottleneck further down the pathway.”
Dr Stephen Harden, the president of the Royal College of Radiologists, said “chronic shortages” of clinical radiologists and clinical oncologists, who diagnose, monitor and treat cancer, were “driving dangerous delays” in diagnosing and treating the disease.
“Perversely, NHS hiring freezes for these doctors have doubled in the last year, making it even harder to keep patients safe,” Harden said. “Technology and new ways of working can relieve pressure to an extent, but fundamentally, rising demand for cancer care has outpaced workforce capacity. The government must now step in to end recruitment freezes and ensure services have the doctors they need to diagnose and treat patients on time.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction, with all three cancer standards better than a year ago, and around 290,000 more people over the last year getting diagnosed on time or having cancer ruled out, compared to the year before the election.
“But we know there is much more to do. Our national cancer plan will help more people to get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner, giving them the best possible chances of recovery and survival.”

Cold weather health alerts issued for parts of UK on Sunday night
UKHSA warns of threat to vulnerable people from frosty conditions expected to last until Thursday
More cold health alerts have been issued for parts of the UK on Sunday night and next week.
The alerts were issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for the north-west, West Midlands and Yorkshire and the Humber, and will be in place from 9pm on Sunday until 9am on Thursday.
These alerts mean the weather is “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, the agency said. The warning came after forecasters predicted the UK was in for a milder weekend, before another cold snap arrives on Monday.
Paul Coleman, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said: “This is the latest cold health alert of the season and we can expect more as we move further into winter.
“Cold weather can have a serious impact on the health of some people, including those aged 65 and over and those with pre-existing health conditions, so it is vital to check in on friends, family and neighbours who are most vulnerable.”
Coleman advised people to heat the rooms they use most and wear warm clothes.
People cross a bridge at St James’s Park in London. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA The Met Office said that on Saturday night, central and easterly parts of England should remain dry with clear spells and a touch of frost, though cloudier conditions are forecast elsewhere as well as some showery rain.
On Sunday, temperatures are expected to not fall below freezing in the morning, with sunshine forecast in the east and across the far north and west as the day progresses.
Conditions are otherwise expected to be fairly bleak with plenty of grey skies, cold breezes and outbreaks of rain, some heavy, and potential hill snow in the north.
A frost covers Wimbledon Common in London on Saturday morning. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock On Monday, colder weather is expected to return. Sunny skies will appear in patches across the UK, while cold showers are forecast to rain down in the north of the UK. Light snow is also expected in hilly areas in the north.
Air pollution soars as fog traps emissions in England’s urban areas
Ethan Douglas, operational meteorologist at the Met Office, told the Press Association: “On Sunday night and Monday morning, there is the potential for some disruptive ice (given the preceding rain and cold night) and snow.
“The snow risk will be constrained to Scottish hills, bringing difficult driving conditions there. The ice risk may be present more widely across the north of the UK, causing extended journey times and potentially hazardous travelling conditions.”
The brighter weather will continue throughout the week, though people should expect declining temperatures, the Met Office said.
On Friday night, temperatures plunged as low as -6.6C in Sennybridge, near Brecon in south Wales, and -6.5C in Shap, a village near Penrith in Cumbria.
The first yellow cold health alerts of the season were issued earlier this week by the UKHSA for the West Midlands and the north-west, and remained in place until noon on Saturday.
